{{Short description|Mapping theorem in topology}}
{{More footnotes needed|date=March 2022}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Lefschetz fixed-point theorem'''<ref name="Lef1926">{{cite journal | first=Solomon|last= Lefschetz|authorlink=Solomon Lefschetz | title=Intersections and transformations of complexes and manifolds | journal=[[Transactions of the American Mathematical Society]] | year=1926 | volume=28 | pages=1–49 | doi=10.2307/1989171 | issue=1|jstor= 1989171|mr=1501331 | doi-access=free }}</ref> is a formula that counts the [[fixed point (mathematics)|fixed point]]s of a [[continuous function (topology)|continuous mapping]] from a [[compact space|compact]] [[triangulable space|triangulable]] [[topological space]] <math>X</math> to itself  by means of [[trace (linear algebra)|trace]]s of the induced mappings on the [[homology group]]s of <math>X</math>. It is named after [[Solomon Lefschetz]], who first stated it in 1926 but in different way involving [[coincidence point]]s of functions.

There are different versions of this theorem: the weak version of theorem shows only existence of fixed point when expression dependent on traces for a mapping is nonzero. The stronger version of theorem, sometimes called '''Lefschetz-Hopf theorem''' counts fixed points with respect to their [[fixed-point index]], provided that their number is finite. There is also [[algebraic geometry]] counterpart of this theorem called '''Lefschetz trace formula''' that allows to express number of points of variety over finite field in terms of action of Frobenius morphism on its cohomologies.

The topological versions of Lefschetz fixed-point theorem are generalizations of other classical results in topology like [[Brouwer fixed-point theorem]] or [[Poincare-Hopf theorem]].

==Historical context==
Lefschetz presented his fixed-point theorem in his 1926 paper about mappings on manifolds{{r|Lef1926}}. Lefschetz's focus was not on fixed points of maps, but rather on what are now called [[coincidence point]]s of maps.

Lefschetz defined coincidence number for two functions as an alternating sum of traces of maps induced on homologies and cohomologies by two functions and isomorphisms arising from Poincare duality for both manifolds. He proved that if this number is nonzero, then <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> must have a coincidence point.

Lefschetz also noted in his paper that assuming <math>X=Y</math> and <math>g=Id_X</math> gives a simpler result, which is now known as the fixed-point theorem.

==Formal statement==
Let <math>f\colon X \rightarrow X\,</math> be a [[continuous map]] from a compact [[triangulable space]] <math>X</math> to itself. Each such map [[singular homology#Functoriality|induces maps]] on [[singular homology|singular homologies]] of <math>X</math>:
:<math>f_*:H_n(X,\mathbb{Q}) \rightarrow H_n(X,\mathbb{Q})</math>
In general case homologies are [[R-module]]s, but since in this case R is a field, homologies are [[vector space]]s and maps induced on them are [[linear map]]s. This allows to define properly a traces of such mappings. 

Now define the '''Lefschetz number'''{{r|EncLNumbers}} of map <math>f</math> as the alternating sum of traces of maps induced on homologies by <math>f</math>:

:<math>\Lambda_f:=\sum_{n = 0}^{\infty}(-1)^{n}\mathrm{tr}(f_*:H_n(X,\mathbb{Q}) \rightarrow H_n(X,\mathbb{Q})),</math>

since for compact and triangulable space from some point the homologies are trivial and traces are zeros, this sum is finite and well-defined.

=== Weak version of theorem===
A simplest version of the Lefschetz fixed-point theorem states that if <math>\Lambda_f \neq 0\,</math>, then <math>f</math> has a fixed point. In other words, there exists <math>x\in X</math> such that <math>f(x)=x</math>.

===Lefschetz–Hopf theorem===
Assume additionally that <math>f</math> has only finitely many fixed points, denote set of this points as <math>\mathrm{Fix}(f)</math>. Let <math>\mathrm{ind}(f,x)</math> denote the [[fixed-point index]] for <math>x\in X</math> and map <math>f:X \rightarrow X</math>. Then holds<ref>{{Cite book | last=Dold | first=Albrecht | authorlink=Albrecht Dold| title=Lectures on algebraic topology | publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]] | location=Berlin, New York | edition=2nd  | isbn=978-3-540-10369-1 |mr=606196 | year=1980 | volume=200 }}, Proposition VII.6.6.</ref>:

:<math>\sum_{x \in \mathrm{Fix}(f)} \mathrm{ind}(f,x) = \Lambda_f,</math>

===Original coincidence theorem===
Assume that <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> be compact and orientable manifolds of the same dimension. Let <math>f,g:X \rightarrow Y</math> be continuous maps. We take maps induced on homologies by <math>f</math>   on homologies in a covariant way:
:<math>f_*:H_n(X,\mathbb{Q}) \rightarrow H_n(Y,\mathbb{Q})</math>
and take a maps induced on cohomologies by <math>g</math> in a contravariant way:
:<math>g^*:H^n(Y,\mathbb{Q}) \rightarrow H^n(X,\mathbb{Q})</math>
For passing between homologies and cohomologies we are using isomorphisms of [[Poincare duality]]  for respectively <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math>:
:<math>D_X:H^n(X,\mathbb{Q}) \rightarrow H_n(X,\mathbb{Q})</math>
:<math>D_Y:H^n(Y,\mathbb{Q}) \rightarrow H_n(Y,\mathbb{Q})</math>
The composition <math>D_X \circ g^* \circ D_Y^{-1} \circ f_*</math> is a linear mapping from <math>H_n(X,\mathbb{Q})</math> to itself.
Then ''Lefschetz coincidence number'' is defined as:
:<math>\Lambda_{f,g} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} (-1)^k \mathrm{tr}( D_X \circ g^* \circ D_Y^{-1} \circ f_*).</math>
In his original paper Lefschetz proved that if <math>\Lambda_{f,g} \neq 0</math>, then <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> must have a coincidence point. In other words, there exists <math>x\in X</math> such that:
<math>f(x) = g(x)</math>

==Remarks==
The converse of Lefschetz theorem is not true in general: <math>\Lambda_f</math> may be zero even if <math>f</math> has fixed points, as is the case for the identity map on odd-dimensional spheres.

Since [[homotopic]] maps induce the same maps on homologies, then Lefschetz numbers are equal for two homotopic maps.

The Lefschetz number<ref name="EncLNumbers">{{cite web|access-date=2025-01-11 |title=Lefschetz number - Encyclopedia of Mathematics |url=https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Lefschetz_number |website=encyclopediaofmath.org}}<!-- auto-translated from Polish by Module:CS1 translator --></ref> of the [[identity function|identity map]] on a finite [[CW complex]] can be easily computed by realizing that each <math>f_\ast</math> can be thought of as an [[identity matrix]], and so each trace term is simply the dimension of the appropriate homology group. Thus the Lefschetz number of the identity map is equal to the alternating sum of the [[Betti number]]s of the space, which in turn is equal to the [[Euler characteristic]] <math>\chi(X)</math>. Thus we have
:<math>\Lambda_{\mathrm{id}} = \chi(X).\ </math>
Consequently, each map homotopic to identity map have Lefschetz number equal to Euler characteristic of <math>X</math>

The same conclusion could be obtained for any compact [[Absolute neighborhood retract]], in particular any compact topological manifold. The basic ingredient behind this extension is that compact Absolute neighborhood retracts are homotopy equivalent to finite simplicial complexes.

==Sketch of a proof==
First, by applying the [[simplicial approximation theorem]], one shows that if <math>f</math> has no fixed points, then (possibly after subdividing <math>X</math>) <math>f</math> is homotopic to a fixed-point-free [[simplicial map]] (i.e., it sends each simplex to a different simplex).  This means that the diagonal values of the matrices of the linear maps induced on the [[Simplicial homology|simplicial chain complex]] of <math>X</math> must all be zero.  Then one notes that, in general, the Lefschetz number can also be computed using the alternating sum of the matrix traces of the aforementioned linear maps.  In the particular case of a fixed-point-free simplicial map, all of the diagonal values are zero, and thus the traces are all zero.

==Consequences==
The different versions of Lefschetz theorem are generalization of classical results in topology.

===Brouwer fixed-point theorem===
{{main|Brouwer fixed-point theorem}}
The Brouwer fixed-point theorem says that if <math>D^n</math> is n-dimensional closed unit disc, then every continuous map <math>f:D^n\rightarrow D^n</math> must have fixed point.<ref name="brouwer-1910">{{cite journal | last1 = Brouwer | first1 = L. E. J. | author-link = Luitzen Egbertus Jan Brouwer | year = 1911| title = Über Abbildungen von Mannigfaltigkeiten | url = http://resolver.sub.uni-goettingen.de/purl?GDZPPN002264021 | journal = [[Mathematische Annalen]] | volume = 71 | pages = 97–115 | doi = 10.1007/BF01456931 | s2cid = 177796823 | language = de }}</ref> 

Since <math>D^n</math> is compact and triangulable space, the condition of Lefschetz theorem applies. The homology groups with rational coefficient for <math>D^n</math> are:
:<math> H_n(D^n,\mathbb{Q}) = \begin{cases} \mathbb{Q} & \text{if} & n = 0 & \\ 0 & \text{if} & n > 0 \end{cases}</math>
Because <math>D^n</math> is convex space, then every map <math>f:D^n\rightarrow D^n</math> is homotopic to each other, particularly identity map. Then:
:<math>\Lambda_{f} = \chi(D^n) = 1</math>
From weak version of Lefschetz theorem <math>f</math> must have a fixed point.

===Poincare-Hopf theorem===
{{main|Poincare-Hopf theorem}}
Poincare-Hopf theorem is a consequence of Lefschetz-Hopf theorem. It says that for a vector <math>v</math> field on a compact differentiable manifold <math>M</math> with isolated zeros holds:
:<math>\sum_{v(x)=0} \operatorname{index}_{x}(v) = \chi(M)</math>
In case of differential manifold with boundary, the vector field is assuned to go along boundary.

Because differential manifold is always triangulable, assumption about space is satisfied. Despite this theorem concerns zeros of vector fields instead of fixed points and indices are defined in a different way, the connection comes from the fact that any [[vector field]] on a compact differential manifold treated as a velocity induces a [[Flow (mathematics)|flow]]:
:<math>\varphi(x,t): M \times [0,\infty) \rightarrow M</math>
in a natural way, where in every local chart on <math>M</math> it is given as a solution of differential equation:
:<math>\frac{\partial \varphi(x,t)}{\partial t} = v(x) \qquad \varphi(x,0) = x</math>
For every <math>t \geq 0</math> map <math>\varphi_t(x):=\varphi(x,t)</math> is homotopic to <math>\varphi_0(x)=Id_M</math>, hence:
:<math>\Lambda_{\varphi_t} = \chi(M)</math>
Clearly zeros of vector field remains fixed points of any <math>\varphi_t</math>. Choosing sufficiently small <math>\varepsilon_0 > 0</math> it can be assured that for <math>\varepsilon > t > 0</math> they will be only fixed points of <math>\varphi_t</math>. The indices of vector field zeros are defined as a degree of map <math>u:\partial D \rightarrow \mathbb{S}^{n-1}</math>, where <math>D</math> is local neighbourhood of <math>x</math> that not contain any other zero of <math>x</math> and is homeomorphic to n-dimensional ball and the map <math>u</math> is given as: 
:<math>u(x)=\frac{v(x)}{\vert v(x)\vert}</math>
For each zero <math>x_i</math> of vector field there exists <math>\varepsilon_i > 0</math> such that for <math>\varepsilon_i > t > 0</math>:
:<math>\operatorname{index}_{x_i}(v) = \mathrm{ind}(\varphi_t,x)</math>
Choosing <math>\varepsilon = \min\lbrace \varepsilon_0, \dots , \varepsilon_n \rbrace</math> we get that for every <math>\varepsilon > t > 0</math> Lefschetz-Hopf theorem equality applied to <math>\varphi_t</math> gives desired result.

==Lefschetz trace formula==
Let <math>X</math> be a variety defined over the [[finite field]] <math>k</math> with <math>q</math> elements and let <math>\bar X</math> be the base change of <math>X</math> to the [[algebraic closure]] of <math>k</math>. The '''[[Frobenius endomorphism]]''' of <math>\bar X</math> (often the ''geometric Frobenius'', or just ''the Frobenius''), denoted by  <math>F_q</math>, maps a point with coordinates <math>x_1,\ldots,x_n</math> to the point with coordinates <math>x_1^q,\ldots,x_n^q</math>. Thus the fixed points of <math>F_q</math> are exactly the points of <math>X</math> with coordinates in <math>k</math>; the set of such points is denoted by <math>X(k)</math>.  The Lefschetz trace formula holds in this context, and reads:

:<math>\#X(k)=\sum_i (-1)^i \mathrm{tr}(F_q^*| H^i_c(\bar{X},\Q_{\ell})).</math>

This formula involves the trace of the Frobenius on the [[étale cohomology]], with compact supports, of <math>\bar X</math> with values in the field of [[p-adic number|<math>\ell</math>-adic numbers]], where <math>\ell</math> is a prime coprime to <math>q</math>.

If <math>X</math> is smooth and [[equidimensionality|equidimensional]], this formula can be rewritten in terms of the ''arithmetic Frobenius'' <math>\Phi_q</math>, which acts as the inverse of <math>F_q</math> on cohomology:

:<math>\#X(k)=q^{\dim X}\sum_i (-1)^i \mathrm{tr}((\Phi_q^{-1})^*| H^i(\bar X,\Q_\ell)).</math>

This formula involves usual cohomology, rather than cohomology with compact supports.

The Lefschetz trace formula can also be generalized to [[algebraic stack]]s over finite fields.
